profile.reading:
TulsaConnect operates two data centers in the Tulsa, Oklahoma area, known as DC-3 and DC-5, and this map point corresponds to the downtown DC-5 building at 110 West 7th Street. A second point on the map sits about 550 meters away and also carries the TulsaConnect name. Since the company names only one downtown facility, both points most likely represent the same building rather than two separate ones, probably reflecting two separate survey passes over the same footprint.

TulsaConnect traces its roots to April 1996, when it began as one of Oklahoma's first internet companies, and formally organized under its current name in October 2001. In April 2012 it became part of the Cross Family of Companies, a privately held, third-generation Oklahoma-owned group whose subsidiaries include Cross Telephone Company, Cimarron Telephone Company, CimTel Cable, Pottawatomie Telephone Company, MBO Networks, and the wireless carrier Bravado Wireless. Since its founding, the company says it has grown from a single data center room with 10 racks to multiple facilities with an aggregate capacity of more than 300 racks.

The downtown DC-5 building draws power from an underground dual-substation AEP feed on what TulsaConnect describes as downtown Tulsa's more storm-resilient underground power bus, with automatic switchgear between substation feeds, true A and B UPS output through Eaton 9395 systems, and an 800-kilowatt Caterpillar diesel generator backed by trailer-mounted portable generators the company says it can bring on site within an hour. Cooling runs on Liebert 2N CRAC units drawing on both chilled-water and air-cooled sources for redundancy, arranged in a hot-aisle containment layout, with clean-agent gas fire suppression throughout. The company states the facility is SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type 2 audited, with biometric entry, escorted access, and continuously recorded, motion-triggered video retained for at least 180 days.

Network connectivity includes redundant 10-gigabit backbone links from Lumen, Zayo, Cox, and Cogent, Juniper edge routers, Cisco core and distribution switching, and direct 10-gigabit fiber interconnects linking Downtown Tulsa, East Tulsa, and Oklahoma City. TulsaConnect markets DC-5 as a production or disaster-recovery site for regional businesses that need carrier-neutral colocation without leaving the Tulsa metro.

reading.body:
TulsaConnect operates DC-5, a downtown Tulsa colocation facility drawing dual-feed power from AEP's underground distribution with automatic switchover, backed by an 800-kilowatt diesel generator and portable generators deployable within an hour. The operator publishes no megawatt capacity figure for this building, only that its two facilities combined hold over 300 racks across DC-3 and DC-5. At a conservative 5 kilowatts per rack for regional colocation, 150 racks at DC-5 would represent roughly 0.75 megawatts of IT load, though this is assumption, not published specification.

The facility holds SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type 2 certifications, indicating it qualifies to host production systems for regional businesses under audit. Network connectivity includes four redundant 10-gigabit carriers, Juniper edge routing, and direct fiber to Oklahoma City and two other Tulsa sites. Cooling uses a mix of chilled-water and air-cooled systems in hot-aisle containment, standard for colocation rather than hyperscale AI infrastructure.

Oklahoma publishes no megawatt capacity from any data center operator, and TulsaConnect DC-5 is not among the nine mapped facilities in the state with any disclosed power figure. This campus matters only to the extent it represents regional colocation demand, not AI compute scaling. It is not positioned as or equipped for the power, density, or cooling profile of modern large-language-model training.
